## Introduction

The standard clustering-based cell type annotation annotates cell clusters by looking up their **marker genes** and assigning each cluster a single discrete label. That approach is intuitive and directly interpretable, but it rests on two assumptions that are not always true for the heart maturation dataset we are analysing:

1.  **Cells belong to one cell type.** A cluster is given a single label, and every cell inside it inherits that label.
2.  **Cell identity is discrete.** Cells are either cardiomyocytes or they are not; there is no notion of a cell that is *partly* a fetal cardiomyocyte and *partly* an adult one.

Another issue of the conventional clustering-based annotation approach is that of 'double-dipping', which has been highlighted by recent statistical literature e.g. [this paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10418557/) and [that paper](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.02.756269v1.full). This problem refers to the inflated statistical significance due to conducting clustering and differential gene test on the same data. This problem will probably be more severe when dealing with fine cell types. 

### A quick simulation of double-dipping

To see the problem, we simulate 1,000 cells from **one** population:
every gene has the same expected expression in every cell, so there are
no real cell types and no real marker genes. We then run the standard
Seurat workflow (cluster, then test for marker genes between clusters).
For comparison, we also test between two groups chosen at random, which
is what a valid test of "no difference" looks like.

```{r double-dipping, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
library(Seurat)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(2026)
n_genes <- 1000
n_cells <- 1000
gene_means <- rgamma(n_genes, shape = 0.5, rate = 0.5)
sim_counts <- matrix(
    rpois(n_genes * n_cells, lambda = gene_means), n_genes, n_cells,
    dimnames = list(paste0("gene", seq_len(n_genes)),
                    paste0("cell", seq_len(n_cells)))
)

sim <- CreateSeuratObject(as(sim_counts, "dgCMatrix")) |>
    NormalizeData(verbose = FALSE) |>
    FindVariableFeatures(verbose = FALSE) |>
    ScaleData(verbose = FALSE) |>
    RunPCA(npcs = 10, verbose = FALSE) |>
    FindNeighbors(dims = 1:10, verbose = FALSE) |>
    FindClusters(resolution = 0.5, verbose = FALSE)
table(Idents(sim))

# Clusters 0 vs 1: clustering and testing on the same data
de_clusters <- FindMarkers(sim, ident.1 = "0", ident.2 = "1",
                           logfc.threshold = 0, min.pct = 0)
# Two random groups: a valid test
sim$random_group <- sample(c("A", "B"), n_cells, replace = TRUE)
de_random <- FindMarkers(sim, ident.1 = "A", ident.2 = "B",
                         group.by = "random_group",
                         logfc.threshold = 0, min.pct = 0)

data.frame(
    comparison    = c("cluster 0 vs cluster 1", "random groups"),
    p_below_0.05  = c(sum(de_clusters$p_val < 0.05), sum(de_random$p_val < 0.05)),
    adj_p_below_0.05 = c(sum(de_clusters$p_val_adj < 0.05),
                         sum(de_random$p_val_adj < 0.05))
)

rbind(data.frame(comparison = "cluster 0 vs cluster 1", p = de_clusters$p_val),
      data.frame(comparison = "random groups", p = de_random$p_val)) |>
    ggplot(aes(p)) +
    geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
    facet_wrap(~ comparison) +
    labs(x = "p-value", y = "Number of genes",
         title = "No gene truly differs between any cells") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

With no real difference, about 5% of genes should have p < 0.05, and the
p-values should be spread evenly between 0 and 1. The random groups
behave like that. Between the two clusters, about four times as many
genes look "significant", and some survive multiple-testing correction:
the clustering split the cells along random noise, and the test then
rediscovers that noise. The same can happen in real data, especially
when clusters are split into fine subtypes that differ only slightly.

Our dataset spans foetal, young and adult heart samples, so many cells — especially cardiomyocytes — are in the middle of a maturation continuum. A discrete label forces each cell into one bin and throws away the very gradient we want to study in Module 2 (pseudotime) and Module 3 (cell-specific co-expression networks).

In this module we use **Φ-Space** ([Mao, Deng & Lê Cao, 2025, *Genome Biology*](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-025-03755-8)) to re-annotate the heart data with *continuous* phenotype scores instead of hard labels. The reference based approach can also alleviate the double-dipping problem in clustering-based approach, since the reference data, where the annotator comes from is different from the query data, on which the annotator is applied.




### From hard labels to soft scores

The core idea of Φ-Space is simple: instead of asking *"which cell type is this cell?"*, ask *"how much does this cell resemble each reference phenotype?"*. For every query cell and every phenotype in the reference atlas, Φ-Space returns a real-valued score. A cell that sits halfway between "foetal cardiomyocyte" and "adult cardiomyocyte" will score positively on both; a cell committed firmly to one identity will score high on one and low on the other.

Under the hood, Φ-Space fits a **partial least squares (PLS)** regression from gene expression in the reference onto a dummy matrix of phenotype labels. The fitted model is then applied to the query, producing one score per cell per phenotype. This matrix of scores, the **phenotype space embedding**, is stored as a `reducedDim` and becomes the substrate for every downstream analysis: visualisation, clustering, marker selection, and trajectory inference.



## Load Libraries and Data

```{r load-libraries}
library(PhiSpace)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(Seurat)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(patchwork)
library(ComplexHeatmap)
```

We need two data objects:

- a **query** — the human heart snRNA-seq data of Sim et al. (2021), already quality-controlled and down-sampled to \~10,000 nuclei, with raw counts and sample / stage / sex metadata.
- a **reference** — an annotated left-ventricle atlas covering the full developmental axis (see the next section for details).

```{r load-data}
seu <- readRDS("../data/afternoon_mvp.rds")
reference <- readRDS("../data/reference_gao2026.rds")

cat("Query (Seurat):\n")
cat("  - cells:", ncol(seu), "\n")
cat("  - genes:", nrow(seu), "\n")
cat("  - metadata:", paste(colnames(seu@meta.data), collapse = ", "), "\n\n")

cat("Reference (SingleCellExperiment):\n")
cat("  - cells:", ncol(reference), "\n")
cat("  - genes:", nrow(reference), "\n")
cat("  - assays:", paste(assayNames(reference), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("  - cell types:", length(unique(reference$final_cell_type)), "\n")
cat("  - age groups:", paste(unique(reference$age_group), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

Φ-Space works with `SingleCellExperiment` (SCE) objects, so we convert the query from Seurat to SCE. The raw counts travel across as the `counts` assay; the cell-level metadata travels across as `colData`.

```{r seurat-to-sce}
query <- as.SingleCellExperiment(seu)
assayNames(query)
head(colData(query)[, c("sample", "group", "sex")])
```

We will also set up a cache folder for intermediate results. Computations that take more than a few seconds are cached to `../results/` so that re-rendering this vignette is fast, and so that workshop participants can download the pre-computed caches directly if they prefer.

```{r cache-setup}
results_dir <- Sys.getenv("SCW_RESULTS", "../results")
dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
```

## Choosing a Reference Dataset

A Φ-Space annotation is only as good as the reference it is built on. For the Sim et al. heart data we need a reference that:

- **covers the full developmental axis** — foetal, paediatric and adult heart, so that every query cell has something biologically sensible to score against;
- **annotates cell types at a useful granularity** — at least the major heart lineages (cardiomyocyte, fibroblast, endothelial, pericyte, immune, epicardial, neuronal)

We use the **Gao et al. 2026** (*Genome Biology*) integrative snRNA-seq atlas of the human left ventricle. It combines 299 donors from eight published studies, spans 8 post-conceptional weeks through ≥60 years, and provides harmonised cell type and age-group annotations. We have pre-filtered it to non-diseased donors and balanced the major cell types by down-sampling; the processing recipe is documented in the original workshop's [`references/HPC_reference_processing.md`](https://github.com/phipsonlab/single_cell_workshop/blob/main/references/HPC_reference_processing.md).

### Exercise 1: Would a single-cell reference work?

Our query is single-*nucleus* RNA-seq, and so is the Gao et al.
reference. Many published heart atlases are single-*cell* RNA-seq
instead. Discuss with your neighbour: could you use a whole-cell
scRNA-seq reference to annotate this snRNA-seq query? What could go
wrong, and how would you check?

<details>
<summary>Some points to consider</summary>

- **Coverage.** A reference can only score cells against phenotypes it
  contains. Adult cardiomyocytes are too large to capture as intact
  cells, so whole-cell heart datasets often have few or none of them,
  which is exactly why Sim et al. sequenced nuclei. A query cell with no
  matching reference phenotype still gets scores, but they can only say
  which of the *available* phenotypes it resembles most.
- **Technology differences.** Nuclei and whole cells capture different
  transcripts. Nuclear data have more unspliced (intronic) reads and
  nuclear-retained RNAs such as *MALAT1*; whole-cell data have more
  mitochondrial and other cytoplasmic transcripts. Genes that differ for
  technical reasons can shift the scores.
- **How to check.** Look at whether well-known markers get the expected
  scores (for example, foetal query cells scoring high on foetal
  phenotypes), compare with a second reference if one exists, and
  consider dropping genes known to differ between nuclei and cells
  (mitochondrial genes, for example) before fitting.

</details>

Two columns from the reference drive everything that follows:

```{r reference-metadata}
table(reference$final_cell_type)
table(reference$age_group)
```

Notice the reference's `age_group` is `fetal / young / middle / old`, while our query's `group` is `fetal / young / adult`. That is fine — Φ-Space will score each query cell against all four reference age groups, and we will use those four scores as a fine-grained read-out of where on the maturation axis each cell sits.

### Zooming in: splitting cardiomyocyte and fibroblast into subtypes

Looking at `final_cell_type` above, **Cardiomyocyte** (\~1,900 cells) and **Fibroblast** (\~1,300 cells) dominate the reference. They are also the two lineages we care about most biologically: cardiomyocytes carry the foetal→adult maturation signal we will trace in Module 2, and fibroblasts reshape the extracellular matrix across development. The Gao 2026 authors further annotated these two lineages into biologically meaningful subclusters (e.g. `Fetal_enriched_metabolic`, `Stressed`, `Interstitial`, `Perivascular` …) — stored in the `cell_type_plus_subcluster` column as `CellType:Subtype` strings.

We therefore build a **fine cell-type column** that keeps every non-CM, non-Fibroblast cell on its broad label, and replaces the CM / Fibroblast labels with the Gao subclusters. Two things happen at once:

1.  **We zoom in on the cells we care about.** When a small number of cell types carry most of the biological signal, it is worth asking Φ-Space to resolve them more finely. Every CM subcluster becomes its own phenotype column in the score matrix, so we can tell a `Fetal_enriched_metabolic` CM from a `Stressed` CM rather than collapsing both into "Cardiomyocyte".
2.  **The reference becomes more balanced.** Splitting the two giant classes into \~8 + \~7 smaller classes brings their per-class counts closer to the rarer lineages (Pericyte, Myeloid, Endothelial, …). PLS over-fits the majority class when the reference is unbalanced, and this split softens that skew for free.

```{r split-subtypes}
ct <- reference$final_cell_type
sub <- reference$cell_type_plus_subcluster
# Replace only the two populous lineages with their subclusters;
# leave the rest on their broad label.
reference$cell_type_fine <- ifelse(
    ct %in% c("Cardiomyocyte", "Fibroblast"),
    sub,
    ct
)

sort(table(reference$cell_type_fine), decreasing = TRUE)
```

Note the alternative we did **not** take: **balanced subsampling**. Instead of splitting the majority classes, you could down-sample them with `PhiSpace::subsample(..., key = "final_cell_type", minCellNum = ...)` so every cell type contributes a comparable number of reference cells. That is the right move when you are happy with the broad-class annotation and simply want fairer PLS training; here we chose to split instead because the CM / Fibroblast subclusters are interesting in their own right. The two approaches can also be combined — split first, then subsample within each fine label.

### A note on very rare phenotypes

Even after splitting, some fine labels are tiny (e.g. `Cardiomyocyte:Senescent` ≈ 4 cells, `Fibroblast:Inflammatory` ≈ 6 cells). Training PLS with a phenotype represented by a handful of cells is a bad bargain: the column it produces in the score matrix is mostly noise, and it still consumes a component in the PLS fit.

`PhiSpace()` exposes a `cellTypeThreshold` argument for exactly this case — set it to, say, `20`, and any phenotype level with fewer than 20 reference cells is dropped before model fitting. We use it below to prune the long tail of the subtype split while keeping every lineage that is biologically well-represented.

## Preparing Reference and Query

Three preparation steps are required before we can run Φ-Space:

1.  **Match normalisation.** Φ-Space does not do batch correction between reference and query; it relies on both being on the same numerical scale.
2.  **Match gene names.** PLS can only use genes present in both datasets. Both datasets here use gene symbols.
3.  **Quality control.** Remove genes with no counts in any query cell. They carry no signal about the query.

### Match normalisation with scran

The reference is stored with a `logcounts` assay; the query carries raw `counts`. To put both on the same numerical scale we apply **scran normalisation** to the query as well, via PhiSpace's `scranTransf()` wrapper. `scranTransf()` computes pool-based size factors with `scran::computeSumFactors()` and then calls `scuttle::logNormCounts()`, storing the result in a `logcounts` assay — the same assay name and the same normalisation family the reference already uses.

```{r scran-transform}
ref_cache   <- file.path(results_dir, "05_reference_scran.rds")
query_cache <- file.path(results_dir, "05_query_scran.rds")

if (file.exists(ref_cache)) {
    reference <- readRDS(ref_cache)
    message("Loaded cached scran-normalised reference from ", ref_cache)
} else {
    # Reference logcounts is already scran-normalised from the HPC prep
    # script — nothing to recompute, just cache for reproducibility.
    saveRDS(reference, ref_cache)
}

if (file.exists(query_cache)) {
    query <- readRDS(query_cache)
    message("Loaded cached scran-normalised query from ", query_cache)
} else {
    query <- scranTransf(query)
    saveRDS(query, query_cache)
}

assayNames(reference)
assayNames(query)
```

Both objects now carry a `logcounts` assay, and that is what Φ-Space will use below (`refAssay = "logcounts"`).

How much does it matter that both use the same normalisation? Exercise 2
at the end of this module lets you test it.

### Keep common genes and remove zero-expression genes

`PhiSpace()` itself keeps only the genes found in both reference and
query, so you don't need to match genes before calling it. We still
subset the query here, because Modules 2 and 3 continue with this query
object and should only see genes that Φ-Space could use. `zeroFeatQC()`
then removes genes with no counts in any query cell.

```{r common-genes}
cat("Reference genes:", nrow(reference), "\n")
cat("Query genes:    ", nrow(query), "\n")

query <- query[intersect(rownames(query), rownames(reference)), ]
query <- zeroFeatQC(query)
dim(query)
```

That leaves about 15,000 genes, plenty for PLS.

## Running Φ-Space

We now fit the PLS model on the reference and project the query into the phenotype space. We ask for two phenotype layers at once:

- `cell_type_fine` — the split label we built above (CM / Fibroblast replaced by their Gao subclusters, everything else on its broad label).
- `age_group` (4 levels) — where on the maturation axis does it sit?

We also pass `cellTypeThreshold = 20` so that phenotype levels represented by fewer than 20 reference cells are dropped before PLS fitting — this trims the long tail of rare CM / Fibroblast subclusters without touching the well-populated ones.

Fitting the model and scoring all 10,000 query cells takes a few seconds,
so we run it live.

```{r run-phispace}
query <- PhiSpace(
    reference         = reference,
    query             = query,
    phenotypes        = c("cell_type_fine", "age_group"),
    refAssay          = "logcounts",
    regMethod         = "PLS",
    center            = TRUE,
    scale             = FALSE,
    cellTypeThreshold = 20
)
```

The phenotype-space embedding is stored as a `reducedDim`:

```{r inspect-scores}
phi_scores <- reducedDim(query, "PhiSpace")
dim(phi_scores)
colnames(phi_scores)
round(phi_scores[1:4, 1:6], 3)
```

Each row is a query cell, each column is a reference phenotype level. Values are column-wise normalised so that the median of each column is zero and the maximum absolute deviation is one — high positive values mean the cell resembles that phenotype, values near zero mean average, and negative values mean the cell is confidently *not* that phenotype.

### On the number of components

Φ-Space defaults `ncomp` to the total number of phenotype levels (here 28). This is a sensible starting point that we have found works well in practice. What we tend to observe is that, when there are many phenotypes (e.g. 60 cell types), setting `ncomp` to the default value (e.g. 60) might be too much. This is because many of these cell types are heavily correlated, hence we do not need as many components to capture all the signal. When this is the case, setting `ncomp` to, say, `30` , might be a better choice.

Another setting is `nfeat`, the number of genes Φ-Space selects to
predict each phenotype. By default it uses all genes. Exercise 3 at the
end of this module asks what changes when you use fewer.

## Exploring the Phenotype Space

### Heatmap of scores grouped by developmental stage

A good first look is a heatmap with query cells as rows (grouped by developmental stage) and reference phenotypes as columns. The expectation is clear: cells from the foetal group should score high on foetal-related reference phenotypes, and similarly for young and adult.

```{r heatmap-scores, fig.height=7}
age_levels <- unique(reference$age_group)
split_phenotype <- ifelse(
    colnames(phi_scores) %in% age_levels, "age group", "cell type"
)

ht <- Heatmap(
    phi_scores,
    name             = "Φ-Space score",
    row_split        = query$group,
    column_split     = split_phenotype,
    cluster_row_slices = FALSE,
    show_row_names   = FALSE,
    show_row_dend    = FALSE,
    show_column_dend = FALSE,
    column_names_rot = 45,
    row_title_rot    = 0
)
draw(ht, heatmap_legend_side = "right")
```

Two patterns should jump out:

- Within the `age group` columns, the diagonal block structure tells you that Φ-Space has correctly recovered the developmental stage of each query cell without ever being told what stage it was from.
- Within the `cell type` columns, the dominant column for most cells is one of the `Cardiomyocyte:` subtypes, as expected for a heart sample — but a subset of cells score high on `Fibroblast:` subtypes, `Endothelial`, `Myeloid`, etc.

### PCA biplot of the phenotype space

The phenotype-space embedding is 17-dimensional. To get a two-dimensional view that still reflects the geometry of the embedding, we apply PCA to the score matrix. Φ-Space ships a `getPC()` helper that returns scores, loadings and variance-explained in one call.

```{r phispace-pca}
pc_res <- getPC(phi_scores, ncomp = 5, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
round(pc_res$props * 100, 1)
```

PC1 and PC2 together explain a large fraction of the variance in phenotype space. We now plot the embedding as a **biplot**: one panel shows the query cells (the `scores`), the other panel shows the reference phenotypes (the `loadings`) in the same 2D basis. Reading the two panels together tells you *why* cells sit where they do — a cell in the positive-PC1 / positive-PC2 quadrant is being pulled there by the phenotypes that load positively on both.

```{r biplot, fig.width=14, fig.height=6}
scores_df <- as.data.frame(pc_res$scores[, 1:2])
colnames(scores_df) <- c("PC1", "PC2")
scores_df$group <- query$group

loadings_df <- as.data.frame(pc_res$loadings[, 1:2])
colnames(loadings_df) <- c("PC1", "PC2")
loadings_df$phenotype <- rownames(loadings_df)
loadings_df$layer <- ifelse(
    loadings_df$phenotype %in% unique(reference$age_group),
    "age group", "cell type"
)

pc1_lab <- sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", pc_res$props[1] * 100)
pc2_lab <- sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", pc_res$props[2] * 100)

p_scores <- ggplot(scores_df, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = group)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    labs(title = "Query cells", x = pc1_lab, y = pc2_lab, colour = "Stage") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1)))

p_loadings <- ggplot(loadings_df, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = layer)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.015, "npc")), alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = phenotype), size = 3.5, vjust = -0.4) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("age group" = "#d95f02", "cell type" = "#1b9e77")) +
    labs(title = "Reference phenotypes (loadings)",
         x = pc1_lab, y = pc2_lab, colour = "Phenotype layer") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_scores + p_loadings
```

This biplot is the single most useful visualisation in Φ-Space. Read it like this:

- **Query cells cluster by stage.** The three stage colours should separate along the PC that is loaded most heavily by `fetal`, `young`, `middle`, `old` — that is the maturation axis we will hand off to slingshot in Module 2.
- **Cell-type phenotypes point to where each lineage lives.** A query cell near a `Cardiomyocyte:*` arrow is a cardiomyocyte; one near a `Fibroblast:*` arrow is a fibroblast. Cells in between the two arrows are transitional / ambiguous and would be assigned inconsistently by a hard classifier.
- **The foetal→adult axis is visible even within cardiomyocytes.** Look at where the `Cardiomyocyte:Fetal_enriched_*` loadings sit relative to the adult-stage CM subclusters — query cardiomyocytes should spread along that direction, which is precisely the trajectory Module 2 will trace.

### Query cells coloured by broad cell type

The stage panel tells us *where each donor group lands* in phenotype space, but not *which lineage* each cell belongs to. To see that, we recolour the same query PCA by the broad cell type derived from the fine Φ-Space call (collapsing every `Fibroblast:*` back to `Fibroblast`, every `Cardiomyocyte:*` to `Cardiomyocyte`, etc.). We use `RColorBrewer`'s `Set1` / `Dark2` — pooled to get enough distinct, high-contrast hues for up to \~12 broad lineages without relying on subtle shade differences.

We colour by the *broad* label rather than the fine one because the fine label has 20+ levels — more than any qualitative palette can distinguish cleanly. If we ever need to visualise at the fine resolution, a `facet_wrap(~ broad)` with the fine label inside each panel is much more legible than a single plot with 20+ colours.

```{r biplot-broad, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
age_levels_biplot <- unique(reference$age_group)
ct_cols_biplot    <- setdiff(colnames(phi_scores), age_levels_biplot)
fine_call         <- getLabels(phi_scores[, ct_cols_biplot])
scores_df$broad   <- sub(":.*$", "", fine_call)

n_broad <- length(unique(scores_df$broad))
broad_palette <- c(
    RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(9, "Set1"),
    RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(8, "Dark2")
)[seq_len(n_broad)]

ggplot(scores_df, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = broad)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = broad_palette) +
    labs(title = "Query cells coloured by broad cell type",
         x = pc1_lab, y = pc2_lab, colour = "Broad cell type") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
    theme(legend.position = "right") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1)))
```

Read this panel against the loadings panel above: each broad-cell-type blob should sit on top of (or adjacent to) the loading arrows of its own subtypes. Cardiomyocyte cells should cluster around the `Cardiomyocyte:*` arrows, fibroblasts around the `Fibroblast:*` arrows, and so on.

## Hard vs Soft Classification

Sometimes you genuinely do need a single label per cell — for example, to tabulate cell-type composition per donor. Φ-Space provides `getLabels()` for exactly this: it picks the column with the highest score for each cell.

```{r hard-labels}
age_cols        <- unique(reference$age_group)
cell_type_cols  <- setdiff(colnames(phi_scores), age_cols)

query$PhiCellType <- getLabels(phi_scores[, cell_type_cols])
query$PhiAge      <- getLabels(phi_scores[, age_cols])

# Broad label: collapse "CellType:Subtype" back to "CellType".
query$PhiCellTypeBroad <- sub(":.*$", "", query$PhiCellType)

table(query$PhiCellType)
table(query$PhiCellTypeBroad)
table(query$group, query$PhiAge)
```

The `group` × `PhiAge` cross-table is a useful sanity check: most foetal query cells should land in the `fetal` reference bin, and most adult query cells in `old` — but the off-diagonal entries are where the teaching is. Those cells are the ones whose continuous scores straddle two age groups.

Let's look at the cardiomyocytes more closely — they are the main interest for Module 2:

```{r cm-score-distribution, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
cm_scores <- phi_scores[query$PhiCellTypeBroad == "Cardiomyocyte", age_cols, drop = FALSE]
cm_df <- as.data.frame(cm_scores) %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("cell") %>%
    mutate(group = query$group[match(cell, colnames(query))]) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_longer(all_of(age_cols), names_to = "age_phenotype",
                        values_to = "score") %>%
    mutate(age_phenotype = factor(age_phenotype,
                                  levels = c("fetal", "young", "middle", "old")))

ggplot(cm_df, aes(age_phenotype, score, fill = group)) +
    geom_violin(scale = "width", alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    labs(x = "Reference age group", y = "Φ-Space score",
         fill = "Query stage",
         title = "Age-group scores for query cardiomyocytes") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 13)
```

Notice that even within a single query stage there is substantial spread along the age-group axis. A hard classifier hides this spread; the continuous scores are exactly what slingshot will exploit to trace a maturation trajectory.

## Exercises: How Robust Are the Scores? (Optional)

Each `PhiSpace()` run takes a few seconds, so you can try different
settings and compare the scores with the ones above. The two helper
functions below do the bookkeeping. Neither changes `query` or
`phi_scores`, so the rest of the workshop is not affected.

```{r exercise-helpers}
# Run Φ-Space with the settings used above; return the score matrix.
phi_run <- function(ref, qry, refAssay = "logcounts", queryAssay = NULL, ...) {
    res <- PhiSpace(
        reference         = ref,
        query             = qry,
        phenotypes        = c("cell_type_fine", "age_group"),
        refAssay          = refAssay,
        queryAssay        = queryAssay,
        regMethod         = "PLS",
        center            = TRUE,
        scale             = FALSE,
        cellTypeThreshold = 20,
        ...
    )
    reducedDim(res, "PhiSpace")[, colnames(phi_scores)]
}

# Compare new scores with the original ones (`phi_scores`):
# - median correlation of the cell-type and age-group score columns;
# - % of cells that get the same broad and fine cell-type label.
compare_scores <- function(new, old = phi_scores) {
    ct <- setdiff(colnames(old), age_cols)
    fine_new <- getLabels(new[, ct])
    fine_old <- getLabels(old[, ct])
    tibble(
        cor_cell_type = median(diag(cor(new[, ct], old[, ct]))),
        cor_age_group = median(diag(cor(new[, age_cols], old[, age_cols]))),
        same_broad_label_pct = 100 * mean(sub(":.*$", "", fine_new) ==
                                          sub(":.*$", "", fine_old)),
        same_fine_label_pct  = 100 * mean(fine_new == fine_old)
    ) |>
        mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 2)))
}

compare_scores(phi_scores)  # sanity check: identical scores
```

### Exercise 2: Does matching normalisation matter?

Φ-Space assumes reference and query are on the same numerical scale.
Find out what happens when they are not. Run Φ-Space three times and
compare each result with `compare_scores()`:

a. Normalise the query with simple library-size normalisation instead of
   scran: `logNormTransf(query, assayName = "counts", targetAssay = "lognorm")`,
   then `phi_run(reference, query_ln, queryAssay = "lognorm")`.
b. Forget to normalise the query: `phi_run(reference, query, queryAssay = "counts")`.
   Read the warning.
c. Replace both datasets with within-cell **ranks** (`RankTransf()`),
   which do not depend on normalisation at all. Subset the reference to
   the query's genes first, so that both rank the same genes.

Which mismatch matters, and which doesn't? Then discuss:

- The reference was normalised with Seurat's **SCTransform** and you
  only have that, while the query uses scran. What would you do?
- The query is **imaging-based spatial** data (a panel of a few hundred
  genes). How would you normalise reference and query?

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>

```{r exercise-normalisation}
# a. library-size log-normalisation instead of scran
query_ln <- logNormTransf(query, assayName = "counts", targetAssay = "lognorm")
scores_ln <- phi_run(reference, query_ln, queryAssay = "lognorm")

# b. raw counts in the query, log counts in the reference
scores_counts <- phi_run(reference, query, queryAssay = "counts")

# c. ranks for both, on the same genes
ref_rank   <- RankTransf(reference[rownames(query), ], assayname = "logcounts")
query_rank <- RankTransf(query, assayname = "counts")
scores_rank <- phi_run(ref_rank, query_rank, refAssay = "rank")

bind_rows(
    "a. library-size log-normalisation" = compare_scores(scores_ln),
    "b. raw counts"                     = compare_scores(scores_counts),
    "c. ranks"                          = compare_scores(scores_rank),
    .id = "query normalisation"
)
```

- **(a) barely matters.** scran and library-size normalisation are both
  log-normalisations of counts, so the scores hardly change.
- **(b) matters a lot.** Raw counts are on a much larger scale than log
  counts, the scores are distorted, and many cells change label.
  Φ-Space warns about this.
- **(c) keeps most of the signal.** Ranks give the same result whatever
  normalisation each dataset had, because normalisation does not change
  the order of genes within a cell. The price is resolution: broad cell
  types are mostly kept, fine subtypes much less.

For the discussion:

- **SCTransform.** SCTransform's `data` layer holds log-transformed
  corrected counts, close to an ordinary log-normalisation, so it can be
  paired with a log-normalised query, as in (a). Its `scale.data` layer
  holds Pearson residuals, which are centred and on a different scale:
  mixing those with log counts is a mismatch like (b). Best is to
  re-normalise both datasets the same way from raw counts; if the
  reference's counts are not available, ranks (c) are a safe fallback.
- **Spatial query.** Use only the genes on the panel, for both datasets,
  and normalise both the same way after subsetting (library-size
  normalisation on a small panel is driven by which genes are on it).
  Ranks are robust here too, because sequencing and imaging detect genes
  with very different efficiencies.

</details>

### Exercise 3: Fewer features

By default, Φ-Space uses all genes. With `nfeat`, it uses only the genes
that matter most for each phenotype, which is similar in spirit to using
only marker (DE) genes. Run `phi_run(reference, query, nfeat = 100)` and
compare the scores with the original ones. Which scores change, and
which don't? Look in particular at the age-group scores of the
cardiomyocytes: does the adult cardiomyocytes' best-matching reference
age group change?

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>

```{r exercise-nfeat, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
scores_nf <- phi_run(reference, query, nfeat = 100)
compare_scores(scores_nf)

# Median age-group score of cardiomyocytes, by query stage
is_cm <- query$PhiCellTypeBroad == "Cardiomyocyte"
age_order <- c("fetal", "young", "middle", "old")
age_medians <- function(scores) {
    apply(scores[is_cm, age_order], 2, \(x) tapply(x, query$group[is_cm], median))
}
list(all_genes = round(age_medians(phi_scores), 2),
     nfeat_100 = round(age_medians(scores_nf), 2))

stage_split <- factor(query$group[is_cm], levels = c("fetal", "young", "adult"))
age_heatmap <- function(scores, title) {
    Heatmap(scores[is_cm, age_order], name = title, column_title = title,
            row_split = stage_split, cluster_columns = FALSE,
            cluster_row_slices = FALSE, show_row_names = FALSE,
            show_row_dend = FALSE, row_title_rot = 0)
}
draw(age_heatmap(phi_scores, "All genes") +
         age_heatmap(scores_nf, "nfeat = 100"))
```

- The **cell-type scores** and the **foetal** score change little: those
  phenotypes differ in many genes, and the top 100 carry the signal.
  Broad labels hardly change; about a fifth of cells change their fine
  subtype label, the most sensitive part of the annotation.
- The **post-natal age-group scores** (`young`, `middle`, `old`) change
  the most. These groups differ in fewer genes, and using all genes
  dilutes them. With 100 genes per phenotype, the adult donors'
  cardiomyocytes move from `young` towards `middle`, closer to their
  true age (35–42 years).

Fewer features help when you need **specificity** between similar
phenotypes. They cost robustness: with fewer genes, each gene's noise
matters more.

</details>

## Handing Off to Module 2

We save the annotated query object so that Module 2 can pick up where we leave off.

```{r save-for-module-6}
final_cache <- file.path(results_dir, "05_phispace_query.rds")
saveRDS(query, final_cache)
cat("Annotated query at", final_cache, "\n")
```

The object now carries:

- `reducedDim(query, "PhiSpace")` — the score matrix (fine cell-type columns + age-group columns).
- `colData(query)$PhiCellType` — discrete *fine* cell-type label (CM / Fibroblast resolved to subtype).
- `colData(query)$PhiCellTypeBroad` — discrete broad cell-type label (CM and Fibroblast subtypes collapsed back).
- `colData(query)$PhiAge` — discrete maturation-stage label.
- all original metadata (`sample`, `group`, `sex`, QC metrics).

In Module 2 we will **subset this object to cardiomyocytes** (using `PhiCellTypeBroad == "Cardiomyocyte"`) and apply **slingshot** to the PhiSpace score matrix. The continuous age-group scores will act as the biological anchor that tells slingshot which end of the trajectory is foetal and which end is adult.

## Summary

- Φ-Space replaces a hard cell-type label with a continuous score per reference phenotype per cell — a natural fit for a dataset that spans a developmental gradient.
- The workflow is four steps: match normalisation (we used scran normalisation on both reference and query), keep common genes, run `PhiSpace()` with one or more phenotype layers, inspect the scores.
- Continuous scores can always be collapsed to a discrete label with `getLabels()`, but the inverse is not possible — preserve the scores for any downstream analysis that benefits from soft assignments (trajectory inference, co-phenotype analysis, gradient visualisation).
- The phenotype-space embedding we saved is the input to Module 2 (pseudotime) and Module 3 (cell-specific co-expression networks).
